The reference evapotranspiration, ETo, provides, thus, a standard to which:
•  evapotranspiration at different periods of the year or in other regions can be compared;
•  evapotranspiration of other crops can be related. The FAO-PM ETo equation uses standard climatological records of solar radiation
(sunshine), air temperature, humidity and wind speed. To ensure the integrity of
computations, the weather measurements should be made at 2 m (or converted to that
height) above an extensive surface of green grass, shading the ground and not short
of water. Wind speed may often be measured at a height other than 2 m, for example,
at 3 m or 10 m, to avoid influences by nearby tall crops. Measurements at those
heights are transformed to an equivalent wind speed at 2 m height using a logarithmic
transformation as shown later. No weather-based evapotranspiration equation can be expected to predict
evapotranspiration perfectly under every climatic situation due to simplification in
formulation and errors in data measurement. It is probable that precision instruments
under excellent environmental and biological management conditions will show
the FAO-PM ETo equation to deviate at times from true measurements of grass
ETo. However, the Expert Consultation agreed to use the hypothetical reference
definition of the FAO-PM ETo equation as the definition for grass ETo when deriving
and expressing crop coefficients.

2. FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation
During the last 25 years, the time between the publication of the first edition of FAO
Paper 56 in 1998 and this second edition, a number of studies have been produced
showing the relatively good accuracy, consistency and dependability of the FAO-PM
ETo equation and of the ET estimates computed as Kc ETo. This indicates that the
values assigned to the resistances of the FAO-PM ETo equation and the standardized
calculation of important parameters were properly selected. It is important, when comparing the FAO-PM ETo equation to ETo measurements,
that the full Penman-Monteith equation (Equation 2.1) and associated equations for
ra and rs (Equations 2.2 and 2.3) must be used to enable accounting for variation in
ET due to variation in height of the grass measured. Variations in measurement height
can significantly change LAI, d and zom and the corresponding ETo measurement and
predicted value. When evaluating results, it should be noted that local environmental
and management factors, such as watering frequency, also affect ETo observations. The FAO-PM ETo equation is a close, simple representation of the physical and
physiological factors governing the evapotranspiration process. By using the FAO-
PM ETo equation, one may calculate crop coefficients at research sites by relating the
measured crop evapotranspiration (ETc) with the calculated ETo, i.e. Kc = ETc/ETo. In the crop coefficient approach, differences in the crop canopy and aerodynamic
resistance relative to the hypothetical reference crop are accounted for within the crop
coefficient. The Kc factor serves as an aggregation of the physical and physiological
differences between crops and the reference definition. 2.4.2 Impacts of advection
Many irrigated areas around the globe are located in semiarid and arid regions where
irrigated agriculture is downwind of extensive regions of dryness. The upwind dry
regions, through surface heating, increase air temperature and dryness to the overlying
air mass. Two types of advection can exist, local advection and regional advection,
where advection is defined as the transport of warmer, drier air onto an irrigated
surface. When warmer, drier air is transported onto an irrigated surface, it increases the
air temperature and decreases the humidity above the irrigated surface as compared to
what would occur in the absence of the advection. The advection will tend to increase
the corresponding ET rate. Local advection
Local advection occurs when a nearby dry field generates warmer air directly upwind
of an adjacent irrigated field. That warmer air can create an increase in ET at the
edges of the downwind irrigated field and into the field for tens of meters. After the
establishment of a new equilibrium boundary layer (EBL) some tens of meters into the
irrigated field, the effects of the local advection are reduced. The definition for ETo given earlier in this chapter describes ETo as the ET from an
extensive surface of well-watered, clipped grass. The extensive surface is specified so
that the impacts of local advection on the edges of a field are made small in proportion
to the total field ET, and so that weather measurements are less influenced by local
advection. The ETo estimate is, thereby, intended to represent the basis for the ET
produced from the majority of a medium to large, irrigated field. That ET is calculated
as Kc ETo. In other words, the ETo estimate represents ET that occurs for the average
well-watered field when surrounded by other agricultural fields that may have low or
high amounts of vegetated cover at various times during the growing season. For this
reason, it is mandatory that weather stations are set up under reference conditions, i.e.
over a well-watered grass field surrounded by other agricultural fields.

Regional advection
Contrary to the impact of local advection, irrigated areas that are downwind of large
areas of dryness, such as in semiarid and arid climates, are influenced by regional
advection. Regional advection transports warmer and drier air from an arid planetary
boundary layer toward an irrigated surface. The transport of warmer and drier air
affects all fields of an irrigated area and is made possible by turbulent eddy transfer. The regional advection impacts the air temperature and humidity gradients above the
irrigated surface, effectively increasing the air temperature and reducing the humidity
at the 2 m height. These changes increase ET from the irrigated surface. The changes
in gradients over the irrigated fields are assumed to be similar to those experienced at a
reference weather station that has a well-watered, transpiring surface and is located in a
similar environment. In those situations, the FAO Penman-Monteith equation responds
to the impacted temperature and humidity gradients established by the weather data
and produces higher ETo. That higher ETo, in turn, corresponds to the higher ET
that occurs from well-watered fields under regional advection. This phenomenon is
common to irrigated fields in arid and semiarid regions and is accurately treated by the
FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation due to its use of solar radiation, air temperature,
air humidity and wind speed measurements. 2.4.3 Data
Apart from the site location, the FAO-PM ETo equation requires air temperature,
humidity, radiation and wind speed data for hourly, daily, weekly, ten-day or monthly
calculations. The computation of all data required for the calculation of the reference
evapotranspiration is given in Chapter 3. Annex 3 presents methods for the completion
of the weather data series and for analysis of the homogeneity of the data series. It is
important to verify the units in which the weather data are reported. Factors to convert
common units to standard unit are presented in Annex 1. Location
The altitude above sea level (m) and latitude (degrees north or south) of the location
should be specified. These data are needed to adjust some weather parameters for the
local average value of atmospheric pressure (a function of the site elevation above mean
sea level) and to compute extraterrestrial radiation (Ra) and, in some cases, daylight
hours (N). In the calculation procedures for Ra and N, the latitude is expressed in
radians (i.e. decimal degrees times π/180). A positive value is used for the northern
hemisphere and a negative value for the southern hemisphere. Temperature
The (average) daily maximum and minimum air temperatures in degrees Celsius
(°C) are required for 24-hour calculation time steps. Where only (average) mean
daily temperatures are available, the calculations can still be executed but some
underestimation of ETo will probably occur due to the non-linearity of the saturation
vapour pressure-temperature relationship. Using mean air temperature instead of
maximum and minimum air temperatures yields a lower saturation vapour pressure
es, and hence a lower vapour pressure difference (es − ea), and a lower reference
evapotranspiration estimate. Air humidity
The (average) daily actual vapour pressure, ea, in kilopascals (kPa) is required. The
actual vapour pressure, where not available, can be derived from maximum and
minimum relative humidity (%), psychrometric data (dry and wet bulb temperatures in
°C) or dewpoint temperature (°C) according to the procedures outlined in Chapter 3.

2. FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation
Solar radiation
The (average) daily net radiation expressed in megajoules per square meter per day
(MJ m-2 day-1) is required. These data are not commonly available but can be derived
from the (average) shortwave radiation measured with a pyranometer or from the
(average) daily actual duration of bright sunshine (hours per day) measured with a
(Campbell-Stokes) sunshine recorder. The use of a sunshine recorder is becoming less
common and a pyranometer is the preferred instrument. The calculation procedures
are outlined in Chapter 3. Wind speed
The (average) daily wind speed in meters per second (m s-1) measured at 2 to 10 m
above the ground level is required. It is important to verify the height at which wind
speed is measured, as wind speeds measured at different heights above the ground
surface differ. The calculation procedure to adjust wind speed to the standard height of
2 m, prior to entry into FAO-PM ETo equation, is presented in Chapter 3. 2.4.4 Missing climatic data
Situations might occur where data for some weather variables are missing. The use of an
alternative ETo calculation procedure, requiring only limited meteorological parameters,
should generally be avoided. It is recommended that one calculates ETo using the
standard FAO-PM ETo method after resolving the specific problem of the missing data. Procedures for estimating missing climatic data are outlined in Chapter 3 with some
material at the end of this Chapter. Differences between ETo values obtained with the
FAO-PM ETo equation with, on the one hand, a limited data set and, on the other hand,
a full data set, are expected, and have been observed to be smaller than or of similar
magnitude to the differences resulting from the use of an alternative ETo equation. Even where the data set contains only maximum and minimum air temperature it is
still possible to obtain reasonable estimates of daily, ten-day or monthly ETo with the
FAO-PM ETo equation. As outlined in Chapter 3, radiation data can be derived from
the air temperature difference, or, along with wind speed and humidity data, can be
imported from a nearby weather station, or from reanalysis weather data, or from
gridded stationary satellite radiation data. Humidity data can be estimated from daily
minimum air temperature. The procedures for estimating missing data should be validated at the regional level. This
can be done for weather stations with full data sets by comparing ETo calculated with
full and with limited data sets. The ratio should be close to one. Where the ratio deviates
significantly from one, the ratio can be used as a correction factor for estimates made
with the limited data set. Where the standard error of estimate exceeds 20 percent of the
mean ETo, a sensitivity analysis should be performed to determine causes (and limits) for
the method utilized to import the missing data. A validation should be completed for
each month and variable for the monthly ETo estimates as well as for the daily estimates. 2.4.5 Importance of utilizing weather data collected over transpiring
(reference) surfaces
The development of the Penman and Penman-Monteith combination equations
eliminated the need to measure or estimate surface temperature and vapour pressure
at the surface by combining the energy balance with the mass transfer method. A
requirement is that the equations should only be applied using standard weather
measurements of air temperature, vapour pressure, solar radiation, and wind speed

collected over transpiring surfaces. The assumptions in the combination equation,
including the calculation of the slope of the vapour pressure curve (Δ) using air
temperature, require that the temperature of the surface be similar to the air temperature,
or within a few degrees. This is usually the case for the reference ETo because ET from
a well-watered grassed surface consumes most of the energy available from Rn and G,
so that sensible heat, H, is small. A small value for H means that differences between
surface temperature and air temperature are also small. Vapour transport from a transpiring surface increases the actual vapour pressure of
the air for several meters above the surface and cools the air temperature. This is in
contrast to a dry, non-transpiring surface, where heating of the surface adds substantial
heat to the air above the surface, but no vapour. The FAO-PM ETo equation requires
that the near-surface boundary layer that resides for several meters above the surface
behaves as that over a transpiring surface where the air temperature is cooled, and
vapour pressure is increased. These expectations carry into the estimation of Δ using air
temperature, the calculation of saturation and actual vapour pressure and net radiation. These calculations all utilize the measured air temperature and vapour pressure values. Applying the combination equation using high temperature and low vapour pressure
measured over a non-transpiring surface confuses the equation by instructing it to
estimate the ET rate that would be required to occur in spite of high air temperature and
low vapour pressure over a transpiring surface. This causes the combination equation
to function under an unrealistic and perhaps even impossible situation. This impossible
situation must be mitigated by limiting weather data sets to those that are collected
over large, well-watered surfaces. Or, for non-conforming weather data sets that are
influenced by the dryness of the measurement site, or by a weather grid-generating
model, the data sets should be corrected by adjusting the near-surface air temperature
and/or humidity data to levels expected and realistic for well-watered conditions. In summary, an important requirement in applying the FAO-PM ETo method to
calculate ETo for irrigated agriculture is the assumption that the surface underlying
the weather measurements is evaporating or transpiring at nearly the same rate as the
ETo calculation produced by the FAO-PM ETo equation. This condition is required
so that the near-surface profiles for air temperature, humidity and wind speed are in
equilibrium with a well-watered surface represented by the FAO-PM ETo. In addition,
the net radiation (Rn) estimate for the standardized FAO-PM ETo equation assumes a
relatively cooled surface having long-wave radiation emission that can be as much as
100 W m-2 less than the long-wave emission associated with a warmer non-evaporating
or non-transpiring surface. The next section describes relatively simple empirical, but effective, procedures to
adjust air temperature and/or humidity (dewpoint temperature) data. That adjustment
or conditioning is done prior to using the weather data in the FAO-PM ETo equation. 2.5 ADJUSTMENT AND CORRECTION OF WEATHER DATA TO
ACCOUNT FOR THE DRYNESS OF THE WEATHER STATION
ENVIRONMENT
The concept on which the FAO-PM ETo method for computing ETo is based requires
that weather data be measured under environmental conditions that correspond to,
and are synchronized with, the definition of reference evapotranspiration. In other
words, the weather data input to the FAO-PM ETo equation are to be measured above
a surface that corresponds to the reference definition: an extensive grass crop that is

actively evapotranspiring, or at least in an environment having healthy transpiring
vegetation that is not short of water. Computing ETo using standardized estimates for
(Rn − G), ra and rs, ETo will be overstated if calculated using air temperature and vapour
pressure data collected in an arid, non-reference setting. A correction is therefore
required to bring temperature and humidity data sets closer to those that would have
been measured under reference conditions. In an environment having healthy vegetation and adequate soil moisture (reference
conditions), minimum air temperature Tmin usually approaches dewpoint temperature,
Tdew. This especially occurs if the wind speed dies down by early morning and when
soil moisture is high. Air temperatures decrease during night-time by evaporative
cooling when vapour pressure deficit (VPD) is positive and due to surface cooling
caused by the emission of long-wave radiation. For reference conditions, simple
relationships can be used to assess whether weather data adhere to reference ET
conditions and to replace measured humidity data when the data have not been
collected under reference ET conditions. For non-reference weather sites and data sets, soil moisture and/or vegetation limitations
cause the ET of the site to be substantially less than ETo. As a result, Tmin may remain
well above the reported Tdew. One cause of this phenomenon is the large “reservoir”
of sensible heat created during daytime in the atmosphere over an arid region that is
transferred towards the dry surface during the night, reducing the effect of cooling
by long wave radiation. This surface warming is sustained by the lack of evaporative
cooling during nighttime due to the lack of soil moisture at a non-reference site. The
result is the air temperature and Tdew measurements that are uncharacteristic of a
transpiring reference site and that provide the FAO-PM equation with a wrong idea of
the underlying ETo. This phenomenon can be observed in Figure 2.4. FIGURE 2.4

2.5.1 Adjustments to weather daily data collected over dry surfaces
Researchers, hydrologists and engineers have long recognized the impact of local
aridity on near-surface weather measurements and the lack of synchronization and
equilibrium of those measurements with that expected to occur over evaporating
surfaces associated with irrigated agriculture. The lack of synchronization and
equilibrium creates a consequent incongruence within ETo equations such as the
standardized FAO-PM ETo as was described in a previous section. Empirical methods have been developed to adjust arid air temperature downward or to
adjust arid vapour pressure upward. Some of the more simple methods are described
in this section. These empirical approaches generally employ linear adjustments based
on observed differences between weather data collected from close-by irrigated and
non-irrigated locations or by differences between daily minimum air temperature
(Tmin) and daily average dewpoint temperature (Tdew). The objective of the adjustments
is to produce a corrected weather data set that best reflects weather conditions to be
obtained in a well-watered, reference-type environment. These are the data expected
by the standardized FAO-PM ETo equation. The following sections describe two procedures for recognizing and correcting nonreference weather data prior to its use to calculate ETo. The second procedure adjusts
both air temperature and dewpoint temperature whereas the first procedure is even
simpler and adjusts dewpoint temperature data only. Both procedures can produce very
helpful adjustments that account for the aridity of a weather station site and the data
collected, and help to bring the data into synchronization with the reference surface. A third type of procedure for adjusting air temperature, humidity and even wind speed
data utilizes a more theoretical boundary layer profile theory. These procedures are still
in their infancy, but may become more commonly used in the future due to their more
physical basis and ability to automatically identify the extent of adjustments needed. 2.5.2 Adjustment to Tdew or ea
A simple, yet relatively effective approach to correct weather data collected in a nonreference setting is to retain the measured air temperature data with no adjustment, but
to abandon the use of all collected humidity data (Tdew, ea or RH). Instead, replacement
humidity data are synthesized to better describe conditions of a reference (wellwatered) environment. The synthesized humidity data set works with the original
reported air temperature data to produce a VPD, (es − ea) that is expected to occur in a
reference weather station environment. An estimate of actual vapour pressure, ea, can be obtained by assuming that the daily
average dewpoint temperature (Tdew) is near the daily minimum temperature (Tmin). This implicitly assumes that at sunrise, when the air temperature is close to Tmin, that
the near-surface air over a well-watered, transpiring surface has cooled, so that it is
nearly saturated with water vapour, and the relative humidity is nearly 100 percent. The relationship Tdew ≈ Tmin holds for locations in humid climates and where the cover
crop of the station is well watered. However, particularly for arid regions, the air might
not be saturated when its temperature is at its minimum due to the entrainment of dry
air from above the irrigated area. Hence, Tmin might remain greater than Tdew and a
further calibration is then recommended to estimate dewpoint temperature. In these situations, Tdew may be estimated from Tmin using subtractive correction
factors, aT, that vary with the general aridity of the surrounding region unless the
weather station is cropped with irrigated green grass. Thus, a general approach is:
Tdew = Tmin - aT

2.5.4 Adjustment of Tmax, Tmin and Tdew
The second empirical method for adjusting arid weather data provides correction to
both air temperature (Tmax and Tmin) and dewpoint temperature in proportion to the
difference (Tmin − Tdew). The difference Tmin − Tdew functions as an indication of the
aridity of the weather station environment. The methodology can be applied with or
without a “trusted” reference station in the region. When a “trusted” reference site is available in the region to compare against
If one is fortunate to have at least one weather station site in a region that is well-watered,
in other words a station that is located within a sizeable irrigated area or a large wetland
area, then one can use Tmin – Tdew relationships from that “trusted” reference station as a
basis to develop adjustment parameters to apply to arid, non-reference weather station
data. The adjustments can also be applied to arid, gridded weather data. In this second procedure, adjustments are split between air temperature and dewpoint
temperature. Monthly, daily or hourly weather data can be corrected using the
following approach:
1. Compare Tmin – Tdew from a suspected non-reference site with that from a trusted
reference site in the same region (if available) using a graphical procedure such as
in Figure 2.4 or 2.5 and using monthly ratios of Precipitation/ETo as the abscissa. Monthly data are utilized to compute Tmin − Tdew and for applying Equation 2.8. 2. For any particular month, when differences Tmin − Tdew for the non-reference
site are systematically more than 2 ºC to 3 oC higher than the Tmin − Tdew for the
reference site, then one can conclude that the non-reference station is impacted by
some degree of aridity and adjustments can be made to the data. One therefore
computes the average difference between the Tmin − Tdew values:
∆Tpaired = (Tmin - Tdew)n/ref - (Tmin - Tdew)ref
(2.8)
where ΔTpaired
upward bias in Tmin – Tdew differences created by non-reference
station aridity [oC],
n/ref
subscript indicating the suspected non-reference weather station,
ref
subscript indicating a “trusted” reference weather station. 3. Corrected daily maximum and minimum air temperatures for each month or day
are calculated using a specified fraction of the ΔTpaired difference:
(Tmax)cor = (Tmax)obs - bT ∆Tpaired
(2.9)
(Tmin)cor = (Tmin)obs - bT ∆Tpaired
(2.10)
where bT
fraction of ΔTpaired correction to be applied to Tmax and Tmin [0 - 1.0],
subscripts cor and obs refer to corrected and observed values. Corrections to Tmax and Tmin are assumed to be the same. These reductions to air
temperature reduce observations by a bT fraction of the distance of the aridity bias in
Tmin – Tdew for the non-reference data. The other (1 – bT) of the bias is added to Tdew in
the following step 4. The default value for bT is 0.3, based on experience. The value 0.3
means that 30 percent of the Tmin – Tdew bias adjusts downward the high values for Tmax
and Tmin and 70 percent of the Tmin – Tdew bias adjusts upward the low values for Tdew.

4. Correction to Tdew:
(Tdew)cor = (Tdew)obs + (1 - bT) ∆Tpaired
(2.11)
The corrections by Equation 2.9 and 2.10 decrease the values for Tmax and Tmin and
corrections by Equation 2.11 increase the value for Tdew. When a “trusted” reference site is not available in the region to compare
against
When there is no reference weather location and data in a region to use to establish
expected relationships between Tmin and Tdew, then the procedure of Equation 2.6 can
be applied using a value for aT from Equation 2.6. First the Tmin – Tdew departure is
calculated for each month:
∆T = Tmin - Tdew
(2.12)
Monthly values can be summed from hourly or daily data as needed. 1. Corrected temperatures for each day (or month) are then calculated as:
(Tmax)cor = (Tmax)obs - bT (∆T - aT)
(2.13)
(Tmin)cor = (Tmin)obs - bT (∆T - aT)
(2.14)
for ΔT > aT, aT is the expected difference estimated using the definitions for aT
following Equation 2.6. If ΔT ≤ aT, then no correction is made to Tmax, Tmin or Tdew. The value bT (~0.3) is the same as for Equations 2.9-2.11, where subscripts "cor"
and "obs" refer to corrected and observed values, respectively. 2. Corrected Tdew for the same months or days is calculated as:
(Tdew)cor = (Tdew)obs + (1 - bT) (∆T - aT)
(2.15)
3. Following corrections, one recomputes ETo using the corrected values for Tmax,
Tmin and Tdew. 2.5.5 Application of aridity corrections to hourly data
Collection of weather data at hourly or shorter time steps is becoming more common
using automated electronic weather stations. In some cases, the calculation of ETo
can be more accurate when using hourly weather data as compared to when using
daily weather data. Therefore, the calculation of ETo using hourly weather data is
encouraged. However, the aridity correction procedures for air temperature and/or
humidity data and QAQC should be equally applied to hourly data. For correction of weather data for hourly or shorter time steps, the procedure begins
by calculating the daily average Tdew data using the hourly data for each day. Tmin and
Tmax are determined by selecting minimum and maximum hourly air temperature values
during the day. The daily average Tdew as well as daily Tmax and Tmin are then averaged
over each month to determine monthly values for ΔTpaired or ΔT using Equation 2.8 or
Equation 2.12. The corrections to hourly air temperature become a single equation
that is applied to each hourly or shorter (or longer) time step for the case of a trusted
reference station:
(Thrly)cor = (Thrly)obs - bT ∆Tpaired
(2.16)

2. FAO Penman-Monteith ETo equation
When a trusted reference station does not exist:
(Thrly)cor = (Thrly)obs - bT (∆T - aT)
(2.17)
The “hrly” subscript refers to hourly or shorter timesteps (or even 3-hour time steps).
ΔTpaired or ΔT are based on 24-hour periods, averaged over each month, even though
corrections are made to hourly or shorter timestep data. Equations 2.15 – 2.17 require
that ΔTpaired > 0 and ΔT-aT > 0. Otherwise, no correction is made. For hourly or shorter time step dewpoint correction, Equation 2.15 is applied to Tdew
of each hourly or shorter time step:
(Tdew hrly)cor = (Tdew hrly)obs + (1 - bT) (∆T - aT)
(2.18)
In other words, the Tair and Tdew for each hourly period during a month are given the
same adjustment. 2.5.6 Gridded weather data sets
Since about the year 2000, the advent of gridded historical weather data derived from
sophisticated land data assimilation system (LDAS) models has provided an alternative
data source to the traditional use of point-based weather station data for estimating
ETo. LDAS systems are principally operated for purposes of weather research and
weather and climate forecasting. LDAS systems are programmed to electronically
assimilate weather data collected from select weather sites around the globe and to
couple those data with land process (soil and vegetation water balance) models and
with atmospheric models to extend the point data and to create gridded weather data
sets that are generally traceable to the original point measurements. Gridded weather data products are made available for the globe from a number
of sources including the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts
(ECMWF) and the European Satellite Applications Facility on Land Surface Analysis
(LSA-SAF) framework. The LSA-SAF framework produces an ETo estimate using a
modified Makkink equation using solar radiation derived from the European Meteosat
Second Generation (MSG) satellite system. In the USA, gridded weather data sets
are produced by NOAA, NASA and NCEP. Many of the gridded weather data sets
include 50-year or longer time periods and have spatial resolutions of 1/6 to 1/8 degree
(~ 9 km x 9 km to 12 km x 12 km) but some gridded data sets have resolutions as large
as 50 km. Time resolutions range from one hour to one day. Many gridded weather
data sets contain daily precipitation, solar radiation, and near surface temperature and
humidity (at ~2 or 3 m reference height), and wind speed often at ~10 m reference
height. These data parameters enable the application of the FAO-PM ETo equation. Figure 2.6 shows four examples of computing the FAO-PM ETo equation from ERA-5
reanalysis of the ECMWF relative to two continental weather station locations and two
island weather station locations. For all cases, the regression coefficients are generally
higher than 1.0, indicating a trend for over-estimation of calculated ETo values, but
the daily error of estimates is lower than 30 percent of the mean daily ETo values. The
exception is the island’s location in altitude (Santa Bárbara, Terceira), which is likely
related to the cloudy and windy climate typical of oceanic islands in altitude. Overall,
the results of using ERA5 reanalysis suggest its appropriateness for use in practice for
these locations in the absence of observed data.

Tendency for aridity artifacts in gridded weather data sets
When used to calculate ETo, LDAS-derived and other assembled data sets should
be reviewed to determine whether the weather data contain substantial “artifacts”
of dryness from the original weather data sets used to drive the LSM models. These artifacts may produce weather data that are characteristic of regional weather
systems, which in semiarid and arid climates, represent the general aridity of the
region. However, for purposes of estimating ETo for use in irrigation-related settings,
the ambient gridded weather data may not exhibit the conditioning effects that

air temperature is reduced and humidity content is increased by the ET supplied by

Generally, the LDAS models creating the gridded data sets are not aware of, and do
not include, irrigation in their daily soil water balances that are used to estimate ET,
and the partitioning of available energy into sensible heat flux, H, and estimation of

2.6 QUALITY ASSURANCE AND QUALITY CONTROL (QAQC)
OF WEATHER DATA
Estimates of reference evapotranspiration (ETo) are no better than weather data upon
which they are based. Assessments of weather data integrity and quality need to be
conducted before data are utilized in ETo equations. Corrections to the data should be
made to account for poor sensor calibration, poor maintenance or for a poor weather
station environment. Some statistics-based corrections for completion of data sets and
for for testing and correction of data sets for homogeneity are described in Annex 3. A cautionary statement in data analysis and application is that “having no data is often
better than having bad data.” Bad data refers to data that are substantially biased or are
faulty, or are not representative of a well-watered environment. When one has no data,
one can look to regional weather or ET data summaries for information that might be
useful to represent conditions within the local area. In the case of “bad” weather data,

also applies to the measurements of evapotranspiration that have been used to develop
or calibrate reference ET equations or to determine crop coefficients. This section presents guidelines to be used to calculate both expected ranges for weather
data measurements and also means to assess integrity of data that fall within the ranges. 2.6.1 Solar radiation using clear sky comparisons
Pyranometer operation and calibration accuracy should be evaluated for a particular
weather location by plotting hourly or daily readings of solar radiation (Rs) against
computed theoretical short-wave radiation that is expected to occur under clear sky
conditions (Rso). Rso can be computed for any day or hour using Equation 3.35 of
Chapter 3 along with calculated Ra. The theoretical Rso should be expected to plot as
an upper envelope of measured Rs. Pyranometers that measure solar radiation can be substantially impacted by a drift
in the sensor calibration caused by aging or film or dust on the sensor. Pyranometers
can also be affected by a lack of level for the sensor. Other error in Rs data can occur
from the use of an incorrect calibration factor to convert millivolts of pyranometer
signal into radiation units. In many situations, faulty Rs data can be corrected by
multiplying by a derived coefficient that is determined using the Rso values. A simple
linear multiplier is often adequate when the problem with sensor reporting is caused
by calibration or dirtiness of the sensor. Daily Rs data
Figure 2.11 shows an example of plotting 24-hour measurements for Rs against the
theoretical Rso calculated using Equation 3.35. The data are taken from the California
Irrigation Management Information System (CIMIS) for a CIMIS station located near
Davis, CA. In the figure, the highest observed values for Rs tend to correspond to the
theoretical envelope of calculated Rso. Those observations represent those on cloudfree days so that pyranometer observations came close to values predicted using the
theoretical Rso curve. One can note that the Rso envelope in Figure 2.11 has day-to-day variations caused
by variation in reported vapour pressure. Those variations impacted the estimation
of precipitable water in the atmosphere. Observed Rs on cloud-free days tended to
increase and decrease with the increases and decreases in Rso. This confirms that the
actual Rs is, in fact, influenced by atmospheric water content. Days 220 to 270 had measured Rs that were consistently close to the Rso curve, but
about 3 to 5 percent below that curve. These appear to have been clear-sky days, but
may have been impacted by some dust or aerosols in the air that increased turbidity
of the atmosphere. It is notable in Figure 2.11 that days during the 180-270 period at
Davis were nearly all clear. This is common for a Mediterranean climate such as exists
for Davis. However, many other regions of the globe will tend to have more cloudimpacted days. Large numbers of cloud-impacted days may increase the difficulty in
identifying enough clear-sky days on which to base an Rs data correction.

Obviously, the corrections based on the computed Rso envelopes presume that the
envelopes are accurate. The accuracy of the Rso envelope may need to be confirmed for
a region by using accurate radiation measurements obtained from a trusted, calibrationgrade pyranometer that has a calibration coefficient that is traceable to the international
standard. The calibration pyranometer should be used only for short term periods of
10 – 14 days, and then should be stored in darkness to extend its life and preserve the
calibrated accuracy. Care should be exercised in the selection of the turbidity coefficient
in Equation 3.35. Unfortunately, little generalized information is available on this factor. 2.6.2 Net radiation
The equations for estimating hourly and 24-hour average rates of net radiation (Rn)
using Rs measurements are generally accurate under most conditions. Therefore,
measured Rn data can be plotted against Rn data that have been estimated using the
equations that are based on measured Rs, air temperature and vapour pressure. The
value for albedo (α) used in the Rn estimating equation should represent conditions of
the surface beneath the radiometer. If measured values for Rn consistently deviate from estimated values by more than 3-5
percent, then the calibration or operation of the Rn device (net radiometer) should be
scrutinized. This type of comparison between measured and calculated Rn can readily
identify days or periods during which the radiometer device has malfunctioned due to
effects of dust, bird droppings, moisture condensation inside plastic domes, deterioration
of the domes, a lack of levelness of the instrument, an electronic malfunction, or a lack
of green vegetation beneath the sensor. Of course, the Rs measurement used in the Rn
equations must also be scrutinized as discussed in the previous section. The user of net radiometer data must be aware that net radiometers manufactured by
different companies may not yield the same measurements of radiation even when
placed over the same surface. These differences are due to differences in sensitivities
of various radiometers to long wave and short-wave radiation and variations among
methods for calibrating sensors during manufacturing. It is important that the type, density and height of vegetation beneath the net radiometer
and the relative soil moisture content be monitored and reported with the data. Care
should be exercised when positioning the radiometer to avoid shading the sensed
vegetation with other instruments or structures and to ensure that the radiometer is not
shaded by other instruments or structures at any time of the day or year. If used to calculate ETo, it is extremely important that measured Rn be taken from a
setting where the net radiometer is placed over a well-watered, green vegetation that has
albedo similar to the grass reference (α = 0.23) and where the vegetation is cooled by the
evapotranspiration process similar to that by the grass reference. Dry, non-transpiring
vegetation or non-evaporating soil can have a surface temperature that is more than
30 oC hotter than that of transpiring vegetation. Entering the hotter temperature into the
Stefan-Boltzmann equation shows that the Rnl for the surface can decrease by as much
as 100 W m-2 (~5 MJ m-2 day-1 and ~0.4 MJ m-2 hour-1). This is caused by the higher
thermally induced long wave emission from the hot, dry surface of nearly 100 W m-2. Use of these data would be in strict violation of the definition for ETo and will cause the
equation to underestimate. In those situations where Rn measurements are not collected
in a reference or near-reference environment, it is highly recommended that one reverts
to using calculated Rn that is based on measured Rs in the ETo calculation.

The accuracy of wind measurements is difficult to assess unless duplicate instruments
are used. One should always scan wind records for the presence of consistently constant
values occurring during periods of low wind speed. For electronic instruments, these
recordings may represent a numerical “offset” in the anemometer calibration equation. The presence of these constant and consistent offsets in the data set indicates either the
presence of exceptionally calm conditions (wind speeds less than about 0.5 m s-1 during
the entire sampling period, which is rare) or malfunctioning of the wind speed sensor
due to electrical shorting or perhaps due to fatigue of bearings. These problems may
not be noticed by the station operator. When possible, a second anemometer of the same design, but with fresh bearings,
should be placed at the weather location for a three- or four-day period at least
once each year, and recordings compared with the permanent instrument. Variations
between recordings can signal a need to replace bearings, switches, or other parts. If a
second data logger is used to record the temporary anemometer, one should be careful
to synchronize data logger clocks. Also, one should be careful that anemometers do not
interfere with one another’s wind stream. Comparisons of wind speed data can be made between two nearby stations using a
double mass balance or other statistical method as described in Annex 3. One should
expect differences between two locations that are time-related or that are caused
by local relief, distance from the ocean and general location. When averaged over
periods of a few weeks to a month, one should expect to see consistent ratios between
two locations. Variation from those consistencies should give cause to look more
closely at wind speed data. As described earlier, anemometer heights should be several meters above surrounding
vegetation. In the case of maize crops or orchards that can grow to more than 3 m, an
anemometer that is located closer than about 20 to 50 m from a cropped field should
be placed at 5 m height or higher. 2.6.5 Relative humidity and vapour pressure
Vapour pressure of air can be difficult to measure accurately. Some older electronic
humidity sensors were commonly plagued by hysteresis, nonlinearity and calibration
errors. Some of these errors are inherent in the sensor design and still plague some
modern sensors. Other errors result from dust, moisture, insects, pollution, and age. As
described earlier, most modern electronic RH sensors are well designed and are less prone
to error. Nevertheless, those sensors can still succumb to age and electronic malfunction. Replication of RH instruments
It is strongly recommended that duplicate RH and air temperature sensors be
permanently employed in electronic weather stations, at least for some period each
year. When duplicate RH and air temperature sensors yield similar measurements,

3. Meteorological variables and parameters
Meteorological variables
and parameters
The methods for calculating evapotranspiration from meteorological data require
climatological inputs and physical parameters. Some data are measured directly at
weather stations. Other parameters are related to commonly measured data and can be
derived with the help of a direct or empirical relationship. This chapter discusses the
source, measurement and computation of all data required for the calculation of the
reference evapotranspiration (ETo) by means of the FAO Penman-Monteith method. Different examples illustrate the various calculation procedures. Meteorological data can be expressed in several units. Conversion factors between
various units and the standard International System of Units (S.I.) are given in Annex 1. Climatic parameters, calculated by means of the equations presented in this chapter are
tabulated and displayed for different meteorological conditions in Annex 2. Only the
standardized relationships are presented in this chapter. Annex 3 proposes procedures
for completing data series and for statistical analysis of weather data. 3.1 METEOROLOGICAL FACTORS DETERMINING ET
The meteorological factors determining evapotranspiration are those weather parameters
that provide energy for vaporization and that remove water vapour from the evaporating
surface. The principal weather parameters to consider are presented below. 3.1.1 Solar radiation
Evapotranspiration involves the transformation of liquid water into vapour. That
process requires large amounts of energy. As a result, the rate of the evapotranspiration
process is determined by the amount of energy available to vaporize water. Solar
radiation is the largest energy source and is able to change large quantities of
liquid water into water vapour. The potential amount of radiation that can reach
the evaporating surface is determined by the location and time of the year. Due
to differences in the position of the sun, the potential radiation differs at various
latitudes, time of day, and during different seasons. The actual solar radiation reaching
the evaporating surface depends on the turbidity of the atmosphere and the presence
of clouds that may reflect and absorb major parts of the radiation. When assessing
the effect of solar radiation on evapotranspiration, one should bear in mind that not
all available energy is used to vaporize water. Part of the solar energy is used to add
warmth to the atmosphere and to the soil profile. 3.1.2 Air temperature
The solar radiation absorbed by the atmosphere and the heat emitted by the surface
increase the air temperature. The sensible heat of the surrounding air can transfer
energy to the crop, if the air is warmer than the surface, and exerts as such a controlling
influence on the rate of evapotranspiration. In sunny, warm weather, the loss of water
by evapotranspiration is greater than in cloudy and cool weather. Chapter 3

3.1.3 Air humidity
While the energy supply from the sun and the surrounding air is the main driving
force for the vaporization of water, the difference between the water vapour pressure
at the evapotranspiring surface and the surrounding air is the determining factor for the
vapour removal. Well-watered fields in hot, dry arid regions consume large amounts of
water due to the abundance of energy and the desiccating power of the dry atmosphere. In humid tropical regions, notwithstanding the high energy input, the high humidity
of the air will reduce the evapotranspiration demand. In such an environment, the air
may already be close to saturation, so that less additional water can be stored in the air
and hence the evapotranspiration rate is lower than in arid regions. 3.1.4 Wind speed
The process of vapour removal depends to a large extent on wind and air turbulence which
transfers large quantities of air over the evaporating surface. When vaporizing water, the
air above the evaporating surface becomes gradually more saturated with water vapour. If this air is not continuously replaced with drier air by turbulence and air movement, the
driving force for water vapour removal and the evapotranspiration rate decrease. The combined effect of climatic factors affecting evapotranspiration is illustrated in

principal weather parameters on evapotranspiration can be assessed with the help

specific characteristic of the atmosphere. Before studying the four principal weather

Concepts
The water content of the air can be expressed in several ways. In agrometeorology,
vapour pressure, dewpoint temperature and relative humidity are common expressions
to indicate air humidity. Vapour pressure
Water vapour is a gas, and its pressure contributes to the total atmospheric pressure. The amount of water in the air is related directly to the partial pressure exerted by the
water vapour in the air and is, therefore, a direct measure of the air water content. When air is enclosed above an evaporating water surface, an equilibrium is reached
between the water molecules escaping and returning to the water reservoir. At that
moment, the air is said to be saturated since it cannot store any extra water molecules. The corresponding pressure is called the saturation vapour pressure (eo(T)). The
number of water molecules that can be stored in the air depends on the temperature
(T). The higher the air temperature, the higher the storage capacity, and the higher its
saturation vapour pressure (Figure 3.2).

As can be seen from Figure 3.2, the slope of the curve changes exponentially with
temperature. At low temperatures, the slope is small and varies only slightly as the
temperature rises. At high temperatures, the slope is large and small changes in T result
in large changes in slope. The slope of the saturation vapour pressure curve, Δ, is an
important parameter in describing vaporization and is required in the equations for
calculating ETo from climatic data. The actual vapour pressure (ea) is the vapour pressure exerted by the actual quantity
of water in the air. When the air is not saturated, the actual vapour pressure will be
lower than the saturation vapour pressure. The difference between the saturation and
actual vapour pressure is called the vapour pressure deficit or saturation deficit and is
an accurate indicator of the actual evaporative capacity of the air. In standard S.I. units, pressure is no longer expressed in centimetre of water, millimetre
of mercury, bars, atmosphere, etc., but in pascals (Pa). Conversion factors between
various units and Pa are given in Annex 1. As a pascal refers to a relatively small force (1
newton) applied on a relatively large surface (1 m2), multiples of the basic unit are often
used. Vapour pressure is expressed in kilopascals (1 kPa = 1 000 Pa). Dewpoint temperature
The dewpoint temperature is the temperature to which the air needs to be cooled to
make the air saturated. The actual vapour pressure of the air is the saturation vapour
pressure at the dewpoint temperature. The drier the air, the larger the difference
between the air temperature and dewpoint temperature. Relative humidity

actual (ea) to the saturation (eo(T)) vapour pressure at the same temperature (T):

Relative humidity is the ratio between the amount of water the ambient air actually
holds and the amount it could hold at the same temperature. It is dimensionless
and is commonly given as a percentage. Although the actual vapour pressure might
be relatively constant throughout the day, the relative humidity fluctuates between
a maximum near sunrise and a minimum around early afternoon (Figure 3.3). The
variation of the relative humidity is the result of the fact that the saturation vapour
pressure is determined by the air temperature. As the temperature changes during the
day, the relative humidity also changes substantially. FIGURE 3.3

3.2.6 Measurement
It is not possible to directly measure the actual vapour pressure. The vapour pressure is
commonly derived from relative humidity or dewpoint temperature. Relative humidity
is measured directly with hygrometers. Older mechanical systems in mechanicallybased field stations used hair hygrometers where the hair changes its length in response
to changes in air humidity. These systems were normally operated as mechanical
hygrographs. Measurements with hair hygrometers tend to lose accuracy with dust and
aging of the hair. Modern electronic hygrometers use films from a dielectric polymer
that changes its dielectric constant with changes in surface moisture, thus inducing a
variation in the capacity of a condensator using that dielectric. These instruments are
normally called dielectric polymer capacitive hygrometers. Accuracy can be higher
than for hair hygrometers, the systems can be fully automated, and modern electronic
sensors require little maintenance. Vapour pressure can be measured indirectly with psychrometers that measure the
temperature difference between two thermometers, the so-called dry and wet bulb
thermometers. The dry bulb thermometer measures the temperature of the air. The
bulb of the wet bulb thermometer is covered with a wick that is kept constantly
saturated with distilled water. Evaporation of water from the wick, requiring energy,
lowers the temperature of the thermometer. The drier the air, the larger the evaporative
cooling and the larger the temperature drop. The difference between the dry and wet

bulb temperatures is called the wet bulb depression and is a measure of the air humidity. Usually, the dry and wet bulb thermometers are swung in the air by hand to produce
sufficient air flow past the bulbs. The Assmann psychrometer has a forced ventilation
of the wet bulb and dry bulb thermometers. When wet and dry bulb instruments are
placed inside a naturally ventilated inside a shelter, problems can arise if air flow is not
sufficient to maintain an appropriate evaporation rate and associated cooling. In more
modern systems, the dry and wet bulb temperatures are measured by thermocouples
or by thermistors, the so-called thermocouple psychrometers and thermo-sound
psychrometers. These psychrometers are used in automatic weather stations and, when
properly maintained and operated, tend to provide accurate measurements. The dewpoint temperature is measured with dewpoint meters. The underlying principle
of some types of apparatus is the cooling of the ambient air until dew formation occurs. The corresponding temperature is the dewpoint temperature. Measurement systems can
use a mirror like metallic surface that is artificially cooled until vapour condenses on it and
blocks the reading of reflected light. Other dew sensor systems use chemical or electric
properties of certain materials that are altered when absorbing water vapour. Instruments
for measuring dew point temperature require careful operation and maintenance and are
seldom available in weather stations. The accuracy of estimation of the actual vapour
pressure from Tdew is generally good under good maintenance protocol. Relative humidity and dewpoint temperature data can be notoriously plagued by
measurement errors. Measurement error is common for both older hygro-thermograph
types of instruments and older electronic instruments prior to about the year 2000. The
more modern electronic instruments since about the year 2000 tend to have improved
dependability, consistency, and accuracy. However, the data collected still must be
reviewed and verified. Great care should be taken to assess the accuracy and integrity of RH and dewpoint
data. The user is encouraged to always compare computed dewpoint temperatures to
daily minimum air temperatures, as described near the end of Chapter 2. Frequently,
it is better to utilize a dewpoint temperature that is estimated from daily minimum air
temperature, rather than to use unreliable relative humidity measurements. The user is
encouraged to utilize good judgement in this area. 3.2.7 Calculation procedures

3.3.1 Concepts
Extraterrestrial radiation (Ra)
The radiation striking a surface perpendicular to the sun’s rays at the top of the earth’s
atmosphere, called the solar constant, is about 0.082 MJ m-2 min-1. The local intensity
of radiation is, however, determined by the angle between the direction of the sun’s
rays and the normal to the surface of the atmosphere. This angle will change during the
day and will be different at different latitudes and during different seasons. The solar
radiation received at the top of the earth’s atmosphere on a horizontal surface is called
the extraterrestrial (solar) or exo-atmospheric radiation, Ra. If the sun is directly overhead, the angle of incidence is zero and the extraterrestrial
radiation is 0.0820 MJ m-2 min-1. As seasons change, the position of the sun, the length
of the day and, hence, Ra change as well. Extraterrestrial radiation is thus a function
of latitude, date and time of day. Daily values of Ra throughout the year for different

3. Meteorological variables and parameters
Solar or shortwave radiation (Rs)
As the radiation penetrates the atmosphere, some of the radiation is scattered, reflected
or absorbed by the atmospheric gases, clouds and dust. The amount of radiation
reaching a horizontal plane is known as the solar radiation, Rs. Because the sun emits
energy by means of electromagnetic waves characterized by short wavelengths, solar
radiation is also referred to as shortwave radiation. For a cloudless day, Rs is roughly 75 percent of extra-terrestrial radiation due to
about 25 percent of Ra absorbed or scattered in the atmosphere. On a cloudy day,
additional radiation is scattered or absorbed by clouds, but even with extremely
dense cloud cover, about 25 percent of the extraterrestrial radiation may still reach the
earth’s surface mainly as diffuse sky radiation. Solar radiation is also known as global
radiation, meaning that it is the sum of direct shortwave radiation from the sun and
diffuse sky radiation from all upward angles. Relative shortwave radiation (Rs/Rso)
The relative shortwave radiation is the ratio of the solar radiation (Rs) to the clear-sky
solar radiation (Rso). Rs is the solar radiation that actually reaches the earth’s surface in
a given period, while Rso is the solar radiation that would reach the same surface during
the same period but under cloudless conditions. The relative shortwave radiation is a way to express the cloudiness of the atmosphere;
the cloudier the sky the smaller the ratio. The ratio varies between about 0.33 (dense
cloud cover) and 1 (clear sky). In the absence of a direct measurement of Rn, the relative
shortwave radiation is used in the computation of the net longwave radiation. Relative sunshine duration (n/N)
The relative sunshine duration is another ratio that expresses the cloudiness of the
atmosphere. It is the ratio of the actual duration of sunshine, n, to the maximum possible
duration of sunshine or daylight hours N. In the absence of any clouds, the actual
duration of sunshine is equal to the daylight hours (n = N) and the ratio is one, while on
completely cloudy days n and, consequently, the ratio may be zero. In the absence of a
direct measurement of Rs, the relative sunshine duration, n/N, can be used to derive solar
radiation from extraterrestrial radiation. As with extraterrestrial radiation, the daylength
N depends on the position of the sun and is hence a function of latitude and date. Daily
values of N throughout the year for different latitudes are plotted in Figure 3.5. FIGURE 3.5

Albedo (α) and net solar radiation (Rns)
A considerable amount of solar radiation reaching the earth’s surface is reflected. The
fraction, α, of the solar radiation reflected by the surface is known as the albedo. The
albedo is highly variable for different surfaces and for the angle of incidence or slope
of the ground surface. It may be as large as 0.95 for freshly fallen snow and as small as
0.05 for wet bare soil or open water. A green vegetation cover has an albedo of about
0.20-0.25. For the green grass reference crop, α is assumed to have a value of 0.23. The
net solar radiation, Rns, is the fraction of the solar radiation Rs that is not reflected from
the surface. Its value is (1 − α)Rs. Net longwave radiation (Rnl)
The solar radiation absorbed by the earth is converted to heat energy. By several processes,
including the emission of radiation, the earth loses this energy. The earth, which is at a
much lower temperature than the sun, emits radiative energy with wavelengths longer
than those from the sun. Therefore, the terrestrial radiation is referred to as longwave
radiation. The emitted longwave radiation (Rl, up) is absorbed by the atmosphere or is
lost into space. As a consequence of the atmosphere being above absolute zero K, the
atmosphere radiates energy of its own, as illustrated in Figure 3.6. Part of the radiation
finds its way back to the earth’s surface. The longwave radiation received at the surface
from the atmosphere (Rl, down) helps to sustain surface temperature. Consequently, the
earth’s surface both emits and receives longwave radiation. The difference between
outgoing and incoming longwave radiation is called the net longwave radiation, Rnl. As
the outgoing longwave radiation is almost always greater than the incoming longwave
radiation, a positive Rnl represents an energy loss from the surface. Net radiation (Rn)
The net radiation, Rn, is the difference between incoming and outgoing radiation
of both short and long wavelengths. It is the balance between the energy absorbed,
reflected, and emitted by the earth’s surface or the difference between the incoming
net shortwave (Rns) and the net outgoing longwave (Rnl) radiation (Figure 3.6). Rn is
normally positive during the daytime and negative during the nighttime. The total
daily value for Rn is almost always positive over a period of 24 hours, except in extreme
conditions at high latitudes. FIGURE 3.6

3. Meteorological variables and parameters
Soil heat flux (G)
In making estimates of evapotranspiration, all terms of the energy balance (Equation
1.1) should be considered. The soil heat flux, G, is the energy that is utilized in heating
the soil. G is positive when the soil is warming and negative when the soil is cooling. Although the soil heat flux is small compared to Rn and may often be ignored, the
amount of energy gained or lost by the soil in this process should theoretically be
subtracted or added to Rn when estimating evapotranspiration. 3.3.2 Units
The standard unit used in this guideline to express energy received on a unit surface
per unit time is megajoules per square meter per day (MJ m-2 day-1) or megajoules per
square meter per hour (MJ m-2 hr-1). For hourly or shorter time periods, radiation
is expressed in (MJ m-2 hr-1) for use in the FAO-PM ETo equation. It may also be
expressed as watts per square meter (W m-2). In some meteorological bulletins, other
units might be used, or radiation might even be expressed in units no longer accepted
as standard S.I. units, such as calories cm-2 day-1. In the 24-hour FAO-PM ETo equation (Equation 2.4), radiation expressed in
MJ m-2 day-1 is converted (Box 3.2) to equivalent evaporation in mm day-1 by using a
conversion factor equal to the inverse of the latent heat of vaporization (1/λ = 0.408):

3.3.3 Measurement
Solar radiation can be measured with pyranometers, radiometers or solarimeters. The instruments contain a sensor installed on a horizontal surface that measures the
intensity of the total solar radiation, i.e. both direct and diffuse radiation from clear
sky and/or cloudy conditions. Solar radiation is most commonly measured with
pyranometers. Pyranometers measure the shortwave incoming radiation over a solid
angle in the shape of a hemisphere oriented upwards. In the most common “glassed dome” pyranometers, a thermopile is used within the
instrument as the sensor, where thermal gradients are measured across hot and cold
areas (black and white) or as conducted into the instrument base (solid black). The
radiation intensity is proportional to the temperature differences between the sensing
areas. Accuracy depends upon the sensitivity and age of the material used in the
sensors, the response time and the distortion characteristics of the material constituting
the dome covering the sensors. A second type of pyranometer that is less expensive and that is gaining acceptance is
the silicon diode instrument where electric current is generated by a photo sensitive
diode in proportion to solar intensity. Ordinarily, silicon diode pyranometers are not
fully sensitive to the full spectrum of visible light, and the calibration of the instrument
is only valid for upward-facing solar measurements. When a pyranometer is oriented downwards it measures the reflected shortwave radiation,
and is thus called an albedometer. When two pyranometers are associated they must have
full sensitivity to all spectra of visible light. This is important since together, with one
oriented upwards and the other downwards, the net short-wave radiation can be measured
by subtracting one reading from the other. The instrument is then called a net pyranometer. A point of caution is that any instrument used as an albedometer or net pyranometer
composition of reflected light from vegetation is biased toward green. Therefore, most
albedometers must be of the glass domed thermopile type and not the photo diode type. Where pyranometers are not available, solar radiation can be estimated from the duration
of bright sunshine. Sunshine duration, n, is most commonly recorded with the Campbell-
Stokes heliograph. This instrument records periods of bright sunshine by using a glass
globe that acts as a lens. The sun rays are concentrated at a focal point that burns a hole
in a specially treated card mounted concentrically with the sphere. The movement of the
sun changes the focal point throughout the day and a trace is burned into the card. If the
sun is obscured, the trace is interrupted. The hours of bright sunshine are indicated by the

incoming longwave and emitted longwave radiation all separately. Four component

be quality assured separately. In addition, upward and downward facing components
can be swapped periodically, for a few moments, by inverting the instrument. This
provides a verification that both shortwave sensors have similar readings and that both
longwave sensors have similar readings. The black bodies of radiometers can lose their sensing capabilities with time, so that
these instruments require regular and frequent calibration. Other net radiometers have
been comprised of ventilated differential thermopiles, but they are seldom utilized. The quantity of heat conducted into the soil, G, can be measured with systems of soil

The net longwave radiation is defined as the difference between longwave radiation
emitted and reflected from the surface and the longwave radiation emitted to the
surface from the atmosphere. The rate of longwave energy emission is proportional
to the absolute temperature of the surface raised to the fourth power. This relation
is expressed quantitatively by the Stefan-Boltzmann law. The net energy flux is less
than that emitted from the earth’s surface due to the absorption and downward
radiation from the sky. Water vapour, clouds, carbon dioxide and dust are absorbers
and emitters of longwave radiation. Their concentrations should be known when
assessing the net outgoing flux. In general, the longwave radiation emitted from the
surface is greater than the longwave radiation emitted to the surface from the sky. This is because, under sunlit conditions, the surface tends to be warmer than the
effective atmospheric temperature. As humidity and cloudiness play an important role,
the Stefan-Boltzmann law is corrected by these two factors when estimating the net
outgoing flux of longwave radiation. It is assumed that the concentrations of the other
absorbers are constant resulting:

3.4 WIND SPEED
3.4.1 Measurement
Wind is characterized by its direction and velocity. Wind direction refers to the
direction from which the wind is blowing. For the computation of evapotranspiration,
wind speed is the relevant variable. As wind speed at a given location varies with time,
it is necessary to express it as an average over a given time interval. Wind speed is given
in meters per second (m s-1) or kilometres per day (km day-1). For the standardized
calculation of evapotranspiration with the PM equation, wind speed measured at 2 m
or transformed to an equivalent wind speed at 2 m above the surface is required. Wind speed is measured with anemometers. The anemometers commonly used in
weather stations are composed of cups or propellers that are turned by the force of
the wind. By counting the number of revolutions over a given time period, the average

sonic anemometers are used. These have the advantage of having no moving parts or
bearings that require maintenance. Measurements by cup and propeller anemometers are reliable provided that maintenance

utilize mechanical counters as the output device. Modern anemometers may be
equipped with generators giving a voltage signal that is proportional to the wind speed. Other anemometers may be equipped with small magnetic reed switches or with optoelectronic couplers that generate electric impulses in proportion to the wind speed. The
electronic devices are utilized in automatic weather stations. Anemometers that collect wind speed data to be used to calculate ETo are always placed
at a height not less than 2 m above the ground, following recommendations by WMO. The accuracy of wind speed measurements depends on the upwind fetch as much as on
instrumentation. A large upwind fetch that is free of buildings and trees is definitely
required for representative measurements. In many agrometeorological weather
stations, it may be preferred to place the anemometer at 3 to 4 m above the ground
surface so that the anemometer has less opportunity to be obstructed or influenced by
tall crops, such as maize, growing in the vicinity. The wind speed measurement is then
adjusted, numerically, to an equivalent wind speed at 2 m (Equation 3.50). 3.4.2 Wind profile relationship

3.5 CLIMATIC DATA ACQUISITION
Meteorological data are recorded at various types of weather stations. Agrometeorological
stations are intended to be sited in cropped areas where instruments are exposed to
atmospheric conditions similar to those for the surrounding crops. In these stations,
air temperature and humidity, wind speed and solar radiation or sunshine duration are
typically measured at 2 m above an extensive surface of grass or short crop. Where
needed and feasible, the cover of the station is irrigated. Guidelines for the establishment
and maintenance of agrometeorological stations are given in the FAO Irrigation
and Drainage Paper No. 27. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has
published, since 1950, the Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMO-
No. 8). The 2021 edition includes several volumes: I: Measurement of Meteorological

Data collected at stations other than agrometeorological stations require a careful
analysis of their validity before their use. For example, in aeronautic stations, data
relevant to aviation are measured. As airports are often situated near urban conditions
and away from irrigated areas, temperatures are often higher than those found in rural
agricultural areas as explained in Chapter 2. Wind speed is commonly measured at 10
m height above the ground surface and needs to be adjusted to the standard 2 m height
for the ETo estimate (Figure 3.7). The country’s national meteorological services should be contacted for information on
the climatic data collected at various types of weather stations in the country. National
services commonly publish meteorological bulletins listing processed climatic data
from the various stations. As described in Chapter 2, gridded weather data sets are
becoming commonly available. It is essential that those data be assessed for quality and
representativeness for use in estimating ETo. 3.6 ESTIMATING MISSING CLIMATIC DATA
The assessment of the reference evapotranspiration with the FAO-PM ETo method
is developed in Chapter 4. The calculation of ETo with the FAO-PM ETo equation
requires hourly, daily, ten-day, or monthly maximum and minimum air temperature
(Tmax and Tmin), actual vapour pressure (ea), net radiation (Rn calculated from Rs) and
wind speed standardized to 2 m (u2). If some of the required weather data are missing or cannot be calculated, it is strongly
recommended that the user estimate the missing climatic data with one of the following
procedures and continue to use the FAO-PM ETo equation. The use of an alternative
ETo calculation procedure, requiring only limited meteorological parameters, is less
recommended. Procedures to estimate missing humidity, solar radiation and wind
speed data are given in this section. 3.6.1 Estimating missing humidity data
Where humidity data are lacking or are of questionable quality, an estimate of actual
vapour pressure, ea, can be obtained by assuming that the dewpoint temperature (Tdew)
is near the daily minimum temperature (Tmin). This statement implicitly assumes that
at sunrise, when the air temperature is close to Tmin, that the near-surface air over
a well-watered, transpiring surface is nearly saturated with water vapour and the
relative humidity is nearly 100 percent. Reasons for this are described in Chapter 2 and
procedures to estimate Tdew are presented in Chapter 2. 3.6.2 Estimating missing radiation data
Net radiation measuring devices, requiring professional control, have rarely been
installed in agrometeorological stations. In the absence of direct measurement, longwave
and net radiation can be derived from more commonly observed weather parameters,
i.e., solar radiation or sunshine hours, air temperature and vapour pressure. Where
solar radiation is not measured, it can be estimated from measured hours of bright
sunshine. However, where daily sunshine hours (n) are not available, solar radiation
data cannot be computed with the calculation procedures previously presented. This
section presents additional alternative methods to estimate solar radiation data. Solar radiation data from a nearby weather station
This method relies on the fact that for the same month and often for the same day, the
variables affecting incoming solar radiation, Rs, and sunshine duration, n, are similar
throughout a given region. This implies or requires that: (i) the size of the region is
small; (ii) the air masses governing rainfall and cloudiness are nearly identical within

should observe climatic conditions in both locations and obtain information from local

similar cloudiness and sunshine durations are related to similarities in temperature
and humidity trends. Related statistical procedures are described in Annex 3. Generally, daily calculations of ETo with estimated radiation data are justified when
utilized as a sum or an average over a several-day period. This is the case for the
computation of the mean evapotranspiration demand between successive irrigations
or when planning irrigation schedules. Under these conditions, the relative error for
one day often counterbalances the error for another day of the averaging period. Daily
estimates should not be utilized as true daily estimates but only in averages over the
period under consideration. Solar radiation data derived from air temperature difference
The difference between the maximum and minimum air temperature is related to the degree
of cloud cover in a location. Clear-sky conditions result in high temperatures during the
day (Tmax), because the atmosphere is transparent to the incoming solar radiation, and in
low temperatures during the night (Tmin), because less downward longwave radiation is
emitted by the atmosphere. On the other hand, in overcast conditions, Tmax is relatively
smaller because a significant part of the incoming solar radiation never reaches the earth’s
surface and is absorbed and reflected by the clouds. Similarly, Tmin will be relatively
higher because the cloud cover acts as a blanket and decreases the net outgoing longwave
radiation. Therefore, the difference between the maximum and minimum air temperature
(Tmax − Tmin) can be used as an indicator of the fraction of extraterrestrial radiation that
reaches the earth’s surface. This principle has been utilized by Hargreaves and Samani to
develop estimates of ETo using only air temperature data.

The Hargreaves-Samani radiation formula, adjusted and validated at several weather
stations in a variety of climate conditions, becomes:
Rs = kRs√ (Tmax - Tmin) Ra

recommended by Hargreaves and Samani as 0.16 for land locations, not influenced

and relates to the atmospheric conditions that influence the availability of incoming
solar radiation at crop and natural surfaces, and so with the availability of energy for
evaporation. Thus, kRs has been shown to vary spatially with site elevation and the
distance to large water bodies. In addition, its value may increase with the aridity of
the site and with wind speed. A useful approach is to estimate kRs values using various
long-term (ideally > 30-years) average weather variables that allow for characterizing
the site location: the difference between the maximum and minimum air temperature
(TD = Tmax −Tmin), RH and u2. In practice, the site averages are computed from available
local observations or from a nearby weather station, where climates should be similar,
when such data are not available locally (Example 3.14). For all types of climates, kRs may be estimated from a global multiple linear regression

Wind speed data from a nearby weather station
Importing wind speed data from a nearby station, as for radiation data, relies on
the fact that the air flow above a “homogeneous” region may have relatively large
variations through the course of a day but small variations when referring to longer
periods or the total for the day. Data from a nearby station may be imported where air
masses are of the same origin or where the same fronts govern air flows in the region
and where the relief is similar. When importing wind speed data from another station, the regional climate, trends
in the variation of other meteorological parameters and relief should be comparable. Strong winds are often associated with low relative humidity and light winds are
common with high relative humidity. Thus, trends in variation of daily maximum
and minimum relative humidities should be similar in both locations. In mountainous
areas, data should not necessarily be imported from the nearest station but from nearby
stations with similar elevation and exposure to the dominant winds. The paired stations
may even vary from one season to another, depending on the dominant winds. Imported wind speed data can be used when making monthly estimates of
evapotranspiration. Daily calculations are justified when utilized as a sum or average
over a several-day period, such as a week or decade. Empirical estimates of monthly wind speed
As the variation in wind speed averaged over monthly periods is relatively small and
fluctuates around average values, monthly values of wind speed may be estimated. The “average” wind speed estimates may be selected from information available for
the regional climate but should take seasonal changes into account. General values are
suggested in Table 3.2. TABLE 3.2

3.6.4 Minimum data requirements: the Penman-Monteith temperature
approach (PMT)
The PMT approach applies the FAO standardized Penman-Monteith equation where solar
radiation, vapour pressure and wind data may be estimated when missing or when found
to be faulty or nonrepresentative. Many of the suggested procedures rely upon maximum
and minimum air temperature measurements. Unfortunately, there is no dependable way
to estimate air temperature when it is missing. Therefore, it is suggested that maximum
and minimum daily air temperature data are the minimum data requirements necessary
to apply the FAO-PM equation. Figure 3.12 presents an example of the successful

for ETo is closer to 1.0 relative to the global regression Equation 3.53, and RMSE is also
smaller. This condition has been observed in most of the analyzed applications. FIGURE 3.12
